Source code → A → Syntax analysis → Code generation → B → Object code

scheme.mark_scheme:
Name: Lexical analysis (1)
Description: converting a stream of individual characters / strings into a sequence of tokens (lexemes); removes spaces and comments; lexical errors are found (1)

questions.title: Follow a statement through the compiler
questions.text:
Explain how the statement below is processed by **each** stage of a compiler.

```c
price = cost * 2;   // add the profit
```

scheme.mark_scheme:
Lexical analysis (max 2): comment and spaces removed (1); lexemes become tokens — price / cost identifiers, = and * operators, 2 number, ; separator; identifiers added to the symbol table (1)
Syntax analysis (max 2): tokens checked against the grammar of an assignment statement (1); parse tree built with * below = / syntax errors reported (1)
Code generation (1): machine instructions produced, e.g. LDA cost, MUL #2, STA price / addresses allocated
Optimisation (1): e.g. multiply by 2 replaced by addition or shift (strength reduction) / redundant instructions removed
[Max 6]

points.criterion: Code generation described for this statement

scheme.model_answer: In lexical analysis the comment and spaces are removed and the statement is split into tokens: price (identifier), = (operator), cost (identifier), * (operator), 2 (number) and ; (separator); price and cost are added to the symbol table. In syntax analysis the tokens are checked against the grammar rule for an assignment, and a parse tree is built with cost * 2 under the = node. In code generation machine instructions are produced, for example LDA cost, MUL #2, STA price, using the addresses from the symbol table. In optimisation the multiplication by 2 can be replaced by a faster shift-left or by adding cost to itself.

summary: The stages a compiler goes through — lexical analysis, syntax analysis, code generation and code optimisation — with tokens, the symbol table, parse trees, intermediate code and common optimisation techniques.

blocks.content: A **compiler** translates the whole **source code** of a high-level program into **object code** (machine code) that the processor can execute. It does this in a sequence of **stages**; each stage takes the output of the previous one.

flowchart TB
  S[Source code] --> L[1 Lexical analysis]
  L -->|tokens| P[2 Syntax analysis]
  P -->|parse tree| G[3 Code generation]
  G -->|intermediate or object code| O[4 Code optimisation]
  O --> OB[Object code / executable]
  ST[(Symbol table)] -.- L
  ST -.- P
  ST -.- G
blocks.caption: The stages of compilation

blocks.title: What each stage does
rows: Removes spaces and comments; splits the code into **tokens**; builds the **symbol table**
Lexical errors: illegal characters, invalid identifiers
Checks the tokens follow the **grammar rules** of the language; builds a **parse tree**
Syntax errors: missing bracket, wrong order of tokens
Makes the code **faster / smaller** without changing what it does

blocks.title: Symbol table
blocks.content: The **symbol table** is a data structure built during lexical analysis and used by every later stage. It stores each **identifier** (variable, constant, function name) with information such as its **data type**, **scope** and **memory address**.

blocks.title: Semantic analysis
blocks.content: Many compilers add **semantic analysis** after syntax analysis: it checks that the program **makes sense** — variables are declared before use and operations have compatible **data types** (e.g. you cannot multiply a string by a Boolean).

The first stage of compilation. The **lexical analyser (lexer / scanner)** reads the source code character by character, **removes white space and comments**, and groups the characters into **lexemes**, which it converts into **tokens**. Identifiers are entered into the **symbol table**.

items.title: Lexeme
items.content: The actual sequence of characters in the source code, e.g. `total`, `=`, `10`.

items.title: Token
items.content: The **category** of a lexeme, sometimes with a value or a pointer to the symbol table, e.g. *Identifier (total)*, *Operator (=)*, *Number (10)*.

blocks.content:
if (x == 10)   // check the counter
    y = y + 1;
blocks.caption: Source code

blocks.title: Tokens produced by the lexical analyser (the comment and spaces are removed)

blocks.content: The lexer reports a **lexical error** when a sequence of characters does not form any valid token: an **illegal character** (`total = 5 @ 3`), an identifier that **starts with a digit** (`2price`), or an **unterminated string** (`"Hello`). It does **not** check whether the tokens are in a sensible order — that is syntax analysis.

The second stage. The **syntax analyser (parser)** receives the **tokens** and checks that they are arranged according to the **grammar rules** (syntax) of the language. It builds a **parse tree** (or **abstract syntax tree**) showing the structure of each statement, and reports **syntax errors**.

blocks.title: What happens during syntax analysis
items: The parser receives its input in the form of **tokens** from the lexical analyser.
It analyses each statement to make sure it **conforms to the rules of grammar** of the language (often written in **BNF**).
It builds a **parse tree / syntax tree** that represents the structure of the statement.
If a statement breaks the rules, it reports a **syntax error** with the line number.

blocks.title: A grammar rule in BNF
blocks.content:
```text
<assignment> ::= <identifier> = <expression> ;
<expression> ::= <term> | <expression> + <term>
<term>       ::= <identifier> | <number>
```
`y = y + 1 ;` follows the rule, so it is accepted. `y = + 1 y ;` breaks it, so a **syntax error** is reported.

flowchart TB
  A["="] --> Y[y]
  A --> P["+"]
  P --> AA[a]
  P --> M["*"]
  M --> B[b]
  M --> C[c]
blocks.caption: Abstract syntax tree for y = a + b * c

blocks.content: The tree shows the **order of operations**: `b * c` is lower in the tree, so it is calculated first, then added to `a`.

blocks.title: Lexical errors vs syntax errors
rows: Characters do not form a valid token
Tokens are valid but in the **wrong order / structure**
Missing `)` or `;`, `if x == 10` without brackets in C, `y = + 1 y;`

blocks.content: The stage in which the compiler uses the parse tree and the symbol table to produce **intermediate code** and then **object code** — machine-code (or assembly) instructions for the target processor. Memory **addresses** are allocated to variables.

blocks.title: From one statement to machine instructions

items.title: What the code generator does
items.content:
- Translates each node of the parse tree into **instructions** of the target machine.
- **Allocates memory locations / registers** to variables and temporary values (using the symbol table).
- Chooses which **machine instructions** to use (e.g. `ADD`, `MUL`, `JMP`).
- Produces **object code**; a **linker** may later join it with library code into an executable.

items.title: Intermediate code
items.content:
- A simple, machine-independent form (e.g. three-address code: at most one operator per line).
- Makes it easier to **optimise** and to produce code for **different processors** from the same front end.

blocks.content:
Source:        if (x == 10) y = y + 1;

Assembly:      LDA x        ; load x into the accumulator
               CMP #10      ; compare with 10
               BNE END      ; if not equal, skip the assignment
               LDA y
               ADD #1
               STA y        ; y = y + 1
       END:    ...
blocks.caption: An IF statement after code generation

blocks.content: The stage that **improves the generated code** so that it **runs faster** and/or **uses fewer resources (memory, storage)** — **without changing the result** of the program.

blocks.title: Common optimisation techniques
rows: Calculates constant expressions at compile time
Replaces a variable that holds a known constant with the value
Removes code that can **never run** or whose result is **never used**
`t = b*c; a = t + d; e = t + f`
Moves a calculation that does not change out of a loop
`for i…: k = w * h; s = s + k*i`
`k = w * h; for i…: s = s + k*i`
Replaces a slow operation with a faster one
Deletes loads and stores that are not needed

blocks.caption: Dead code elimination — the compiler removes the lines that can never run or have no effect

items.title: Advantages of optimisation
items.content:
- The program **runs faster** — fewer instructions are executed.
- The object code is **smaller** — uses less memory and storage.
- Uses **less power** — important for mobile and embedded devices.

items.title: Disadvantages
items.content:
- Compilation takes **longer**.
- Optimised code is **harder to debug** — it no longer matches the source line by line.
- An incorrect optimisation could introduce errors (rare).

blocks.content: In questions that show a code fragment, look for: **code after `return`** or an **`if` that is always false** → *dead code elimination*; **arithmetic on constants** → *constant folding*; the **same expression twice** → *common sub-expression elimination*; something **inside a loop that never changes** → *loop-invariant code motion*.

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: Name and describe compilation stage A (between source code and syntax analysis). [2]**
Name: **Lexical analysis** (1). Description: the stream of characters is converted into a sequence of **tokens** / white space and comments are removed (1).

**Q: Name and describe stage B (after code generation). [2]**
Name: **Code optimisation** (1). Description: the code is improved to **consume fewer resources and increase execution speed** (1).

**Q: Name the compilation stage that produces the table *Keyword – if, Bracket – (, Identifier – x, Operator – ==, Number – 10*. [1]**
**Lexical analysis.**

**Q: Describe what happens at the stage of syntax analysis. [2]**
The syntax analyser receives its input in the form of **tokens** (1) and analyses the statements to ensure they **conform to the rules of grammar** of the language, building a parse tree / reporting syntax errors (1).

**Q: Name the optimisation used when statements after `return` are removed. [1]**
**Dead code elimination.**

- Putting the stages in the wrong order — it is **lexical → syntax → code generation → optimisation**.
- Saying lexical analysis "checks the grammar" — it only makes **tokens**; grammar is checked in **syntax analysis**.
- Saying optimisation "removes errors" — it makes **correct** code faster or smaller.
- Confusing the **lexeme** (the characters) with the **token** (its category).
- Forgetting the **symbol table** when describing lexical analysis.
